sources.title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India
sources.edition: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton, 2014

claims.subject: vedic
claims.summary: The hymn voice asks the Maruts to set aside their anger and forgive the speaker after Soma intended for them was given away.
claims.speaker: Agastya according to hymn attribution and editorial speaker division
claims.note: Speaker divisions are an editorial reconstruction; the hymn itself does not identify each speech by speaker name.

claims.subject: vedic
claims.summary: The speaker asks Indra and the Maruts to be reconciled and prosper together.
claims.speaker: Agastya according to hymn attribution and editorial speaker division
claims.note: The object Indra is paired with the Maruts in the passage; predicate describes the requested action.

claims.subject: indra
claims.summary: Agastya says to Indra that the Maruts are Indra’s brothers.
claims.speaker: Agastya in the editorial speaker division
claims.note: This wording is in 1.170.2, not 1.171.2; attribution of the speech is based on editorial verse divisions.

claims.subject: vedic
claims.summary: The verse asks Indra together with the Maruts to grant fame and strength to the sons of Māna; the commentary identifies Māna as Agastya’s father.
claims.speaker: Agastya by hymn attribution
claims.note: The verse names a collective, not Māna as the recipient. Jamison–Brereton identify Māna as Agastya’s father in commentary (p. 370); do not automatically identify him with Māna in RV 7.33.13.

claims.subject: vedic
claims.summary: Jamison and Brereton read 1.165, 1.170, and 1.171 together as a poetic sequence about Agastya’s offering and a dispute between Indra and the Maruts.
claims.note: This is a modern reconstruction of a story across hymns, not an explicit continuous narrative in one passage.

claims.subject: vedic
claims.locator: Ṛgveda 1.165, speaker divisions and introduction, pp. 360–361
claims.summary: In the editorial division of 1.165, the closing verses assigned to Agastya address the Maruts and offer them his hymn.
claims.speaker: Agastya according to hymn attribution and editorial speaker division
claims.note: Jamison–Brereton assign 1.165.13–15 to Agastya; the dialogue structure and individual speakers are editorially analyzed.

claims.subject: vedic
claims.summary: The three-verse Marut hymn 1.172 is identified in the edition as a short pendant to Agastya’s Indra–Marut hymn cycle.
claims.note: Traditional/editorial hymn attribution does not establish personal authorship or a historical encounter.

claims.subject: mitra
claims.summary: The translation calls the lightning-radiance seen by Mitra and Varuṇa one of Vasiṣṭha’s births, and mentions another when Agastya brings him to the clan.
claims.note: Jamison–Brereton render this as one of two births; Griffith renders “one and only birth.” This claim follows the former without asserting historical biography.

claims.subject: varuna
claims.summary: The translation calls the lightning-radiance seen by Mitra and Varuṇa one of Vasiṣṭha’s births, and mentions another when Agastya brings him to the clan.
claims.note: Jamison–Brereton render this as one of two births; Griffith renders “one and only birth.” This claim follows the former without asserting historical biography.

claims.subject: vasistha
claims.summary: Griffith translates Vasiṣṭha as the son of Varuṇa and Mitra.
claims.note: The verse belongs to a layered mythic account and does not establish historical parentage.

claims.subject: vasistha
claims.summary: The verse describes Vasiṣṭha as born from Urvaśī, from her mind.
claims.note: Griffith instead renders the passage “Born of their love for Urvasi”; the wording here follows Jamison–Brereton.

claims.subject: vasistha
claims.summary: The verse calls Agastya bringing Vasiṣṭha here for the clan another of Vasiṣṭha’s births.
claims.note: Jamison–Brereton render viśa as “clan”; Griffith says Agastya brought him hither from his stock.

claims.subject: mitra
claims.summary: The hymn says the two gods poured their seed together into a vessel during a ritual gathering.
claims.note: The verse then names Māna as arising from the middle and says that the sage Vasiṣṭha was born from him; do not equate Māna with Agastya.

claims.subject: vedic
claims.summary: The verse associates the Aśvins’ restoration of Viśpalā with praise and poetic formulation by Agastya.
claims.note: The verse mentions Agastya in the third person; it does not say that he met Viśpalā or personally witnessed the event.

claims.subject: asvins
claims.summary: The hymn says the Aśvins reconstituted or restored Viśpalā.
claims.note: The identity and referent of Viśpalā are debated; retain the name without asserting she was a woman, horse, or prosthesis recipient.

findings: RV 1.170 already depicts Indra confronting Agastya over an offering; Jamison–Brereton connect it with 1.165 and 1.171 as a cycle.
open_questions: Dialogue speaker division and whether the three hymns preserve one coherent episode are editorial reconstructions.

findings: RV 1.171 has the attributed Agastya voice plead with the Maruts to forgive and reconcile with Indra; RV 1.172 is a related short hymn.
open_questions: Do not treat the reconstructed ritual story as a historical event.

findings: RV 1.179 is already covered in the graph as a marital dialogue with Agastya.
open_questions: The speaker labels are editorial/traditional; no additional independent Vedic passage connecting her to Agastya was verified in this collection.
A possible Lopāmudrā interpretation of RV 1.170.4’s dual verb is discussed by Jamison–Brereton, p. 370; left unclaimed because the text does not name her there.

findings: RV 7.33.10–13 links Agastya to Vasiṣṭha’s birth imagery, and elaborates layered Mitra–Varuṇa–Urvaśī imagery.
open_questions: The poetry's multiple birth formulations should not be made into a literal chronology or an asserted historical sibling relationship.

findings: RV 7.33.10–13 pairs Mitra with Varuṇa in Vasiṣṭha's birth imagery.
open_questions: The hymn does not offer a historical chronology for divine or sage figures.

findings: RV 7.33.10–13 pairs Varuṇa with Mitra in Vasiṣṭha's birth imagery.
open_questions: No direct Agastya–Varuṇa relation beyond the Vasiṣṭha passage was added here.

findings: RV 7.33.11 describes Vasiṣṭha as born from Urvaśī's mind.
open_questions: This is one element of a layered poetic account; it does not establish a historical parentage or date.

findings: RV 1.180.8 already says Agastya roused the Aśvins with praise.
RV 1.117.11 links their restoration of Viśpalā with Agastya’s praise/formulation.
open_questions: This pass did not verify further primary-text connections beyond the existing graph entry.
Viśpalā’s referent is debated; the new claim preserves that ambiguity.

findings: RV 1.180.4, in a hymn attributed to Agastya, recalls the Aśvins' aid to Atri.
RV 1.117.3 additionally recalls the Aśvins freeing Atri from a narrow place/cleft, in a hymn that separately mentions Agastya at 1.117.11.
open_questions: It is a precedent mentioned by the hymn, not evidence of an encounter between Atri and Agastya.
This is a one-hymn association; it does not establish a personal meeting between Atri and Agastya.

findings: RV 1.180.5, in a hymn attributed to Agastya, recalls the Aśvins' rescue of Tugra's son.
RV 1.117.15 also recalls the Aśvins rescuing Tugra’s son, separate from the Agastya verse at 1.117.11.
open_questions: The wording does not itself securely identify Tugra's son with a particular named figure such as Bhujyu.
Jamison–Brereton identify Tugra’s son with Bhujyu in their translation; this remains an editorial identification rather than an explicit name in 1.117.15.
No direct Vedic passage connecting Trasadasyu with Agastya was verified in this bounded collection; the epic Trasadasyu should not be merged with Vedic names without evidence.
No directly relevant Agastya–Purukutsa connection was verified; no new graph claim is made.

search_log.query: Jamison Brereton Rigveda 1.165 1.170 1.171 Agastya Maruts translation commentary
search_log.outcome: Inspected the accessible 2014 translation/commentary; it explicitly discusses the three-hymn sequence, its inferred story, and editorial voice assignments.

search_log.query: Rigveda 7.33.10–13 Mitra Varuna Urvasi Agastya Vasistha translation
search_log.outcome: Inspected the metrical Sanskrit text at UT Austin and existing Griffith translation source record; verses 10–13 contain the birth imagery and named figures summarized above.

search_log.query: Rigveda Agastya Trasadasyu Purukutsa direct connection
search_log.outcome: No direct relevant connection verified in inspected sources; left as an open question rather than adding claims.

search_log.query: Rigveda 1.117.11 Agastya Viśpalā Aśvins translation and Viśpalā referent
search_log.outcome: Inspected Jamison–Brereton 2014 verse and translation; Agastya’s formulation is connected to the Aśvins restoring Viśpalā. Debate over the Viśpalā referent remains explicitly unresolved.
